title: Declare transformer and fault-current boundaries
lead: A current value without its voltage, power base and network boundary is easy to misuse. This lesson builds a small equivalent circuit in layers, then shows how changing an assumption changes a fault-current screen. The purpose is to expose model limits before equipment selection, not to turn an attractive fault animation into a completed short-circuit study.
objectives: Calculate consistent three-phase current and impedance bases.
Compare infinite- and finite-source fault estimates.
Keep continuous, peak, interrupting and thermal duties distinct.

sections.title: Choose consistent bases
sections.body: For total three-phase apparent power S and line-to-line voltage V, base impedance is V²/S and full-load current is S/(√3 V). Percentage impedance must be divided by 100 on its stated base. The source contribution and transformer contribution cannot be added as unrelated percentages. Complex impedances normally require separate resistance and reactance; the teaching comparison explicitly adopts purely reactive values.

sections.title: Build the two-megavolt-ampere example
sections.body: At 2 MVA, 400 V and 6% impedance, full-load current is 2,886.75 A, base impedance is 0.08 Ω and transformer impedance is 0.0048 Ω. With an infinite source, the simplified three-phase fault is about 48.11 kA. Adding an illustrative 250 MVA source strength contributes 0.00064 Ω and reduces the screen to about 42.45 kA. Both calculations omit the actual cable route and equipment tolerances.

sections.title: Read the missing-duty list
sections.body: The initial symmetrical RMS fault is not the asymmetric peak or the current at interruption. Earth faults require the actual grounding and zero-sequence paths. Minimum faults under weak-source or inverter operation can be harder to detect even when maximum duty is lower. The manuscript also preserves a conflict between a 25 kA note, a 26.2 kA duty and a 31.5 kA schedule; one favourable schedule entry does not reconcile the whole design.

challenge.question: What changes when the upstream source is idealized as infinite?
challenge.answer: The source impedance becomes zero and the fault estimate rises from approximately 42.45 kA to 48.11 kA. This is a changed assumption, not a better measurement.

instructions: Read the declared boundary and units. Predict the selected result before calculating.
Run the starting case and inspect the ledger, assumptions and model limits.
Apply the challenge, run again, and explain the difference. Export only the last completed inputs and results.

scene.title: The layered equivalent circuit
storyboard: Reveal the source, transformer and route as separate blocks.
Expose each impedance with units and base.
Trigger a user-selected three-phase fault marker; update the model-derived RMS value.
Open distinct duty cards for RMS, peak, interruption and minimum detection.
scene.interaction: Toggle finite/infinite source and inspect missing model contributions; do not animate arcing or imply safe working distances.

assessments.question: Find full-load and infinite-source fault current for 1.6 MVA, 400 V and 6%.
assessments.answer: 2,309.40 A full load; 38.49 kA fault under the simplified model.
assessments.rubric: Correct total-three-phase base and percentage conversion.

assessments.question: Convert per-unit impedance to a new apparent-power base at unchanged voltage.
assessments.rubric: Keep the physical ohmic impedance unchanged.

assessments.question: Why can a larger transformer improve capacity but worsen fault duty?
assessments.answer: At fixed voltage and percentage impedance, higher MVA raises rated current and lowers ohmic impedance.
assessments.rubric: Identify which quantities were held fixed.

limits: Purely reactive, bolted three-phase model; voltage factor is 1.
No zero-sequence, motor, cable, tolerance, protection-setting or breaker-selection result.
